newsitem.title: GERMANY: German city takes on phone giant Deutsche Telekom.
newsitem.headline: German city takes on phone giant Deutsche Telekom.

text.p: Local telecommunications operator NetCologne GmbH said on Tuesday it would launch a city-wide online service next week and outlined long-term plans to capture a big piece of the local telephone market.

The company groups the telecommunications activities of three municipal companies in the western German city of Cologne and exemplifies the type of trench warfare facing phone giant Deutsche Telekom when markets are opened next year.
"We want to capture 20 percent of the city's telecommunications market by the year 2004," NetCologne managing director Werner Hanf told a news conference in Bonn.
NetCologne will expand its Internet services next week and launch "Columbus", an online city guide that offers access to government services and local businesses and entertainment.

It already offers local customers Internet access, electronic mail, a home page on the World Wide Web, Internet-based phone services, as well as corporate network services. Its home page on the Web is http://www.NetCologne.de.
It plans to invest 300 million marks ($191.6 million) over the next 10 years to expand its local network to cover the city centre, outlying industry and eventually the entire greater Cologne region.

Its strategy is to build out a so-called "full service network" -- high-speed optical fibre lines that make it possible to merge cable television, Internet and basic telephone services in one network.

Hanf predicted that Telekom could lose another 20 percent of the Cologne market to other competitors such as DBKom GmbH, the joint venture of Mannesmann, railway Deutsche Bahn and AT&T Corp or the joint venture between Veba, RWE and Cable and Wireless.
The German telecoms market is expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks by 2000. Analysts estimate Telekom's share of the market could fall to around 70 percent by then.

Cologne itself has just under one million inhabitants. It is a major centre for the arts, commerce and the media, hosting Germany's leading commercial broadcaster RTL television and industry giants like the German subsidiary of Ford.

While its size is not impressive, NetCologne is just one of over a dozen city networks that are entering the local communications market to offer basic phone service, corporate networks, Internet access and cable television.

The city networks often have substantial local networks that will allow them to take on Telekom in a door-to-door battle for local customers. They could also dove-tail with long-distance networks of bigger players in strategic partnerships and have a significant impact on Telekom.
"It is our goal is to be able to offer comprehensive and quality telephone services on January 1, 1998," Hanf said.

NetCologne is owned by three municipal companies: utility Gas-, Elektrizitaets- und Wasserwerke AG, largest shareholder with 64.9 percent, and Cologne banks Stadtsparkasse, 25.1 percent, and Kreissparkasse, 10 percent.
Some industry observers have complained that municipal companies would replace Telekom with a local monopoly.

"We will watch closely to make sure there is not combining of resources from their monopoly businesses. If there is a clear separation, then we see no reason to get involved," said Franz Masson, director of telecoms regulation in the federal post and telecommunications ministry.
